notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1384.tmp1384.opp-lat: Footnote marks (a, b, c) in the printed text have been omitted. Obs. 3: 'Casalis Benedicti' taken as La Chaise-Dieu (Casa Dei). Obs. 4: 'praetactus' read as 'praefectus'. Obs. 5: 'Columbam' read as 'Columbani', 'Luxovien is' as 'Luxoviensis', 'Eustasli' as 'Eustasii'; the punctuation of the sentence beginning 'Jonas Bobiensis' is faulty in the edition and has been read as a new sentence whose verb is 'haud meminit'. Prologue: the Daniel reference should be 12:3; 'polyandro' (literally 'common burial place') rendered 'tomb'. Book 1.3: the sentence 'Nam etsi juvenilis...' is elliptical; the bracketed words supply the implied subject. Book 1.5: 'eum fierent' read as 'cum fierent'. Book 1.7: 'veritae' read as 'veritas'; the text says 'in Genesis' but the quotation is from Exodus (10:21-23, cited by the edition as X, 20). The reference numbering skips section 2 in the edition.

§8: 'Leviticae sortis officium' is the diaconate. §9: 'triduana ministratio' understood as three days' provisions. §10: 'ditabitur' makes no sense; read as 'ducebatur' or similar (sank towards death). §12: 'mortalem' prefect perhaps for 'mortiferum'; 'matulae' glossed by the edition as 'storeae' (mat). Simon = Simon Magus (simony).

17: ‘fame (??)reamortuus’ is garbled; read as ‘paene mortuus’ (almost dead). 18: ‘Virisionensium’ unidentified; stray ‘a’ omitted. 20: ‘Cura crucis’ read as ‘Cum crucis’. 21: ‘reperti gesti’ and ‘igneus collis’ are obscure; translated literally. 22: ‘immensae altitudinis’ taken with the flames. 24: the prince is unnamed here; footnote letters omitted.

§26: 'uni fex' read as 'uni ex'; 'lure' as 'luce'; 'conhibito' as 'cohibito'/'convocato' (assembled). The subject of 'suscepit' at the end of §26 is ambiguous; taken as Wlfelentus. §28 'perplectere' read as 'perplectere/perstringere' (weave together). §30 'ci' read as 'ei'. §31 'ita evanuit' seems to end abruptly; possibly something is missing.

§32: 'Ut erat impudens et delusio miserabilis' is awkward; rendered as referring to the preceding demonic deception. 'ad eum tandem per spiritum… sensit ministrum' is syntactically disordered; translated by sense. §33: 'Dein quie : ubique cum esset' appears corrupt (perhaps 'Deinde quia ubique esset'); translated by conjecture. 'tenni' read as 'tenui'. §34: 'manc' read as 'mane'; 'creduliter' taken as 'as is believed'. §37: 'Matth. V, 9' presumably should be V, 19. Stray footnote marks (a, b) omitted. 'petalum' is the high-priestly gold plate (cf. Exodus 28:36). §38: the long sentence is anacoluthic; a governing verb such as 'had' is supplied.

§42: 'Navis' plays on the name of the monastery of Nave (Navense monasterium); 'ob portum navigii' is obscure. §43: 'labe' is glossed by the edition as perhaps 'lapsu' ('flow'); translated so. The last clause ('quam divino ministerio usque hodie instinctum fovet pabulum') is awkward; 'instinctum' perhaps for 'extinctum' or 'instructum'. Stray letters b, c, a are footnote marks and are omitted.

nodes.text: IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 640. SAINT SULPICIUS, SURNAMED PIUS, BISHOP OF BOURGES.
THE LIFE OF SAINT SULPICIUS PIUS, BY AN ANONYMOUS MONK OF SAINT-SULPICE, ALMOST HIS CONTEMPORARY.
(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order, from manuscript codices, and in John Bolland.)
PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

1. Besides Sulpicius surnamed Severus, bishop of Bourges, whom some wrongly confuse with Sulpicius Severus, the disciple of Saint Martin, the Church of Bourges had another prelate by the name of Sulpicius, called Pius, whose Life we present here. The former flourished towards the end of the sixth century, the latter at the beginning of the seventh.

2. Two contemporary writers committed the Life of Sulpicius Pius to writing: one at greater length, and he a monk of the monastery built by Sulpicius, whom he repeatedly calls his own patron; the other more briefly, whom we shall therefore call the abridger. John Bolland published both, under 17 January. Here we shall give only the former, noting in its proper place anything in the other worth observing. The monk of Saint-Sulpice indicates his own date at nos. 4, 11, 16, 17 and 32, and to the Life he wrote he added a book of Miracles, which he had promised at the end of the Life of Saint Sulpicius, although the style of the book of Miracles, falling into metrical cadences and flagging throughout, seems to savour of a quite different author, as does the prologue placed before the Life, which is missing in a great many manuscripts. The writer of the Patriarchium Bituricense states that five books on the Life and Miracles of this same Saint Sulpicius are kept in the archives of the treasury of the cathedral church at Bourges; and you should not suppose their author to be other than ours, whose work we have noticed divided into five books in some copies, as may be seen noted in the margin.

3. The work of the monk of Saint-Sulpice was embellished by John Phernandus, a monk of La Chaise-Dieu, praised by Trithemius in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, and inserted in the Patriarchium Bituricense, chapter 31, from whom we shall borrow a few points to illustrate the anonymous author. We pass over Vincent of Beauvais and Saint Antoninus, who, together with many modern writers, have treated of Saint Sulpicius.

4. Usuard and Ado commend Sulpicius in their Martyrologies, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February. Ado's words are worth noting: At Bourges, the deposition of blessed Sulpicius, bishop and confessor, who, educated in letters from boyhood and conspicuous for the light of a holy way of life, shone with virtues even as a layman. Afterwards also, having laid aside his hair, he became father of monks, and, raised from there to the episcopal throne, renowned for his life, he rested in peace. For Sulpicius was the camp abbot, set over the monks who performed the divine offices night and day in the royal camp.

5. Sulpicius was, then, a monk, and indeed both before and after his episcopate; for he gave up pastoral government some years before his death, so as to be free for God in the monastery of Nave which he had founded. But a monk of what institute, in the end? Those who stubbornly maintain the separation of Saint Columbanus' Rule from the Benedictine throughout that whole century will not easily take Sulpicius away from us. In the time of Waldebert, abbot of Luxeuil, and therefore of Sulpicius, monasteries were founded only according to the rule of Saints Benedict and Columbanus, as the weighty and contemporary writer of the Life of Saint Salaberga testifies. Jonas, monk of Bobbio, in the Life of Saint Eustasius, abbot, given above under the year 625, while he lists the monasteries built among the Bituriges according to the prescription of Saint Columbanus, makes no mention of the monastery of Nave, or of Saint-Sulpice, which then existed, no doubt because it obeyed the genuine and pure institutes of Saint Benedict.
THE AUTHOR'S PROLOGUE.

1. Since, by the gift of the eternal Emperor and on account of the merits of the kindly prelate, the hall of the Church is filled with a bright and radiant heap, while the lamp of his virtues gleams, although we are less than fit to speak of worthy things, we nevertheless attempt to bring at least a slender discourse to the ears of the devout people, especially since it is a profit to the hearers to recount with the pen the deeds of faithful men for the remembrance of the peoples. And although the just man, whose name is already contained on the heavenly page, needs nothing from the writing of mortals, yet increases of faith grow up when recent examples of the saints are retold, when to the Christ-worshipping company the shepherd enclosed in paradise is represented by the pen on earth, and the flock, summoned by his examples, may make its way to heaven, so that, according to the oracle of Daniel (Dan. 12:5), both the people, taught by the teaching of their patron, may shine like the splendour of the firmament, and the teacher, with starry light heaped upon him, may gleam; especially since, to declare his merit, in the vast expanse of Gaul, among the abundant matter of his miracles, by the signal gift of Christ, a spring of oil continually overflows with heavenly dew at his sacred body, and so the fire takes perpetual nourishment, in such a way that, by the infusion of the Holy Spirit, the liquid receives continual increase. And although, for this wise man, death extinguished his poor body in payment of nature's debt, yet living miracles shine at his tomb.
THE BOOK BEGINS.

1. Blessed Sulpicius, then, born of distinguished parents, almost among the foremost citizens, and brought up in the royal camp, was the outstanding shepherd of the city of Bourges, and now, by his glorious departure, has been made its patron. In the flower of his early youth, having broken the snares of the world, he took up the service of Christ with a persevering resolve, and the blessed man, while still a little boy, had so burned with the purpose of embracing religion that (if I may say so) had the time of persecution not been lacking, he would of his own accord have thrown himself headlong into dangers. From then on he began to devote himself to readings from the divine books and to exercise himself remarkably in the teachings of the faith. Further, to restrain youthful desires and to gain advances in wisdom, he bound himself with prayers and the reins of abstinence; and the Church's rule was so honoured by him in observance from his very cradle that the crowds of many young and old men who flocked to him, asking about the religion of our faith, he not only converted to the faith but also formed in the precepts of the perfect life.

3. Divine grace was clearly present with him, through which he provoked countless people to imitate him in the faith of God. Above all, he judged that the precepts of the Gospel and the voice of the Saviour were to be fulfilled with the greatest love and zeal. For although [this] might perhaps have seemed [the decision] of a youthful and less mature mind, yet, containing the token of most perfect chastity, he laid it in his soul like a first foundation. And so at length he went on to build the other virtues upon it, and namely in accordance with the faith of the Gospels, in which the exhortation is uttered by the voice of the Saviour that there are eunuchs who have castrated themselves for the kingdom of God (Matt. 19:12), he spurned the bond of marriage and held to his resolve of chastity.

4. Certainly, as far as we have learned from the account of those who were his companions or servants from his boyhood up to our own times, while still placed in secular dress he was seen to do nothing else than build monasteries, raise up basilicas, restore ruined churches with new work, bring help to the wretched, supply necessities from his own wealth to the poor and needy, and free many of the ruined from chains, punishments and squalor, not only by the word and exhortation of perfect and spiritual teaching but also by his own services and ministrations.

5. There was a certain church not far from his parents' house, almost destroyed by enemies, where there was no throng of clergy or people. Since the blessed man made frequent gains of prayer there, he, wishing to avoid touching the kindling of boastfulness, when the deep silences of night came, would secretly put on the garments that penitents customarily wear and, armed with holy prayers, go to spend the night [there]; and when, with sleep scorned for holy labour, sweet meditation was completed, and the splendour of rosy light was illuminating the world, he would again put on the coverings of secular men, and so took pains to conceal his holy resolve. These were his first boyish elements, this the play of his childhood; such was the love towards the Lord that grew up with him.

6. One night in the church of which we spoke, while he was keeping vigil with two boys and was bent low in prayer, and the whole delight of his mind hung on deeper things, two most foul, monstrous spirits, like Ethiopians in face, each seized one of the boys and strove to drag them violently from the church. At length the man of God found his boys behind him, wailing with great cries. He looks upon the foul ones, raises his hand against the adversaries, and as they, now dragging the boys away by force, were snatching them to get outside, the holy man of God brings forth the banner of the cross. At once, the foul and bloody ones having slipped away, the boys remained unharmed. From that time, therefore, that rival of all goodness, enemy of truth and foe of human salvation, turning all his efforts against the soldier of God, strove to frighten with phantasmal threats the man he could not corrupt in mind. If anyone wishes to learn of this more thoroughly, we shall show it briefly a little later in its proper places.

7. Meanwhile he began to become famous for signs and to be adorned with miracles of power. For while still placed in secular dress he healed the sick by prayer and put demons to flight by a word, toiling with all his strength as an athlete of Christ never to depart from his holy resolve. This he wished to keep hidden from human favour, lest any breath of this world's favour should break out and stain his ears with the pollution of arrogance. So, when these things were being done by him, and through the goodness of his deeds the truth of our God was made known by a kind of silent preaching; and when, as commonly happens, the splendour of light kindled some who believed piously, while the foul darkness of cloudy faithlessness overspread others who disparaged impiously, so that what is written in Genesis seemed fulfilled, that for the Egyptians there was thick and palpable darkness, but for the children of Israel there was light in all their dwellings (Exod. 10:20), our God nevertheless goes on being magnified in his saint and extending the work of the power begun with more prosperous successes.

8. And when the report of him had suddenly been scattered far and wide, and, travelling especially through the region that lies under the western sky, had flown abroad, Austregisilus, bishop of the city of Bourges, asked Prince Theoderic that leave be given him to grant [Sulpicius] a share in teaching in the church, because multitudes were flocking to him for the grace of his teaching; and without delay royal authority was conveyed that, his hair cut off, he should take up the burden of the clerical state. And as the grades followed one upon another, having been set over the others for a year and more, he obtained the office of the Levitical lot and ministered to the church.

9. Meanwhile he was girded more and more with the grace of signs; and when Prince Chlothar had been persuaded by the faithful, he at once asked the bishop that leave be given, for his own safety and that of his army, for the blessed man to perform the office of abbot in his camp. Then, when provisions for three days were supplied for himself and all his men, he kept enough for one day and gave out the rest to the needy. And when his men muttered for fear of want, he said: 'Fix the eyes of your mind, my sons, on the Lord the Saviour. Seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all things will be added to you. Remember that prophetic word: But those who seek the Lord shall not lack any good thing (Ps. 33:11).' Indeed, such an abundance of food was suddenly sent to him by the faithful that he could not unreasonably rejoice to have received, without human glory, that hundredfold interest which the faithful Rewarder had promised to his disciples (Matt. 19:29).

10. At length, after a few days had passed, the king was struck by a cruel illness, and, with the poison spread through his limbs, he hastened headlong towards death. Meanwhile the queen, struck by sudden grief, cast away her necklaces, tore her garments, rent her hair and cheeks, and wept for her husband as though already lost. The house was in turmoil; the tears of the maidservants were joined to the laments of their mistress. Indeed they ran together to the most blessed man, clung to his knees and watered his feet with holy tears, that the holy priest might pour out prayer to the Lord for the king's recovery. He, whose hope rested in almighty God, watered his face with weeping and, beating his breast, drew out sick sighs, kept up vigils and fasts, and poured out prayers continually for the sick man. When five days had passed, the king sank ever more steeply towards death. Then the priest was asked by his companions to take a small amount of food to temper his excessive fasting. 'I will not eat,' he said, 'until I can obtain the prince's recovery from Christ the Lord, whom I serve.' And when they kept crying out that, with the prince's breath already failing and he nearly lifeless, he was afflicting his innocent body in vain by long fasting, he, whose salvation endured firmly in God, promised that when seven days were completed the prince, having recovered his former strength, would take food with him and the other companions. And so the day awaited in everyone's prayers arrived: the priest's promises were fulfilled, swift healing was granted to the prince, the priest was lifted up by the hands of all in glorious triumph, and was summoned to the royal banquet with great honours. Through this indeed he was dear and welcome to all.

11. And since we have set down in writing, with the same faith as they reached us, the deeds of the blessed man that we learned from our elders who were his contemporaries, let us now make a beginning from what we saw partly in our own time, and partly from what was handed down to us by our fellow disciples, and leave it to the memory of posterity.

12. So when the king's court was blooming with the fair beauty of the flowers of his virtues and the grace and jewels of his signs, and he had shone out upon this world like a kind of splendour of light and filled far and wide with the fragrance of his scent, it came about that the holy bishop (of whom we made mention a little above) departed to the Lord by a glorious passing. And when the whole people of the church had come together to elect a bishop, and one shouted for one man and another for another, as usually happens in such cases, and a certain part of the more senseless crowd, through the favour of clients, gave consent to certain of the leading men, and through a mortal and insolent prefect, with endless weights of gold and silver, had brought petitions for the king's consent, so that, according to that sacrilegious sect of the unspeakable Simon, they might snatch heavenly grace against all right and law; our people, however, to whom the Saviour says: Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom (Luke 12:32), asked from the immortal Christ and perfect God that the blessed man should be their priest; nevertheless they sent a slender form of embassy with few words, and through one of those of whom it is said: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 5:3), they laid it open to the king's ears. And when he, as commonly happens, infected with the poison of human greed, had his mind bent towards the abundant money brought to him, his wife, kindled with divine love, admonished her husband, crying out that it would be fitting and just, after the passing of so great and such a man, to grant his see to this man, who, of equal merit, was supported by like distinction in the signs of miracles and the grace of virtues. And the glorious woman also recalled to her husband's memory with what labour, by his prayer, he had a little before drawn him back from the precipice of death. At length, by heavenly indulgence, the prince drew counsel from deeper within, and, having checked the poison of greed and spurned the persuasions of the wicked, ordered without delay that what had pleased divine providence be carried out. And so, by the Lord's arrangement, he was found worthy of the first see of Aquitaine at the summit of the episcopate. For it was God's will that a swift conversion should call back peoples divided among themselves and dissenting minds to love of the bishop, and suddenly bind them together in one consent.

13. So the blessed Sulpicius, having obtained the pontifical dignity, bowed beneath the burden, not the honour; indeed he became all things to all, seeking not what was useful to himself but what was useful to many, that they might be saved. And at once the Lord hastened to kindle his priest like a lamp. For the blessed man gave himself up wholly to very great abstinence, unceasing fasts and almost continual vigils; so that if ever natural necessity demanded a little sleep, he did not take it on a soft bed, which he was never accustomed to use, but laid it on the surface of only a mat and a hair-cloth. The venerable man, worthy of God, being distinguished in all things by purity of life and virtues of soul, did not set great value on ornament of speech, because there was in him a soul adorned with divine virtues, and with it the grace of signs which had been granted him by the Lord Jesus Christ, increasing daily the preaching of the word of God and sowing the saving seeds of the kingdom of heaven ever more widely through all the land.

14. Soon indeed he made such progress in amending the people of the Jews, infected with ancient poisons, that they seemed to themselves to behold as it were a new light of truth. And since the teacher of religion taught much by words but more by examples, and they did not see him command his disciples anything he had not first done himself, he without delay allowed no Jew to live without the grace of baptism in the city entrusted to him from heaven. For when he prayed to the Lord continually for their conversion, and taught them that through baptism they had remission of sins and could not otherwise enter the kingdom of God, as if the rays of the true sun had shone into their hearts, they were astonished, and beholding the glory of God with unveiled face, repenting of their old errors, coming with faithful confession, they were baptized by the bishop himself. So by divine gift the outstanding warrior snatched the prey from the enemy. He restored [it] to its Author; from the inmost recesses of the heart he drove out the stain of unbelief by the love of Christ. Some of them live today in the religion of our faith.

15. For after a short time so great a grace of powers increased in him that signs were done through him no less than formerly through the apostles. For whereas we said a little above that he put demons to flight by a word and healed the sick by prayer, our God went further in being magnified in his saint, so that in the course of time he gave back sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, speech to the mute, life to the dead, right hands to the maimed, walking to the lame, and very many other things which it would be long to recount one by one, of which, if God's favour helps, we wish to touch briefly on a few. Come then, my discourse, [do] what you promise.

16. A certain Gunthoald laid his son, about ten years old, whose tongue so clung to his throat that no formed speech had ever come from his mouth, before the feet of the blessed man, and made known the whole case. He, moved with human compassion, with groans and sighs stretched both his eyes and his palms to heaven, calling upon Christ, who is God over all, with all faith and shedding tears; and, having first prayed, he touched the boy's tongue and impressed on it the sign of the cross. At once the tongue was loosed, and to this day he speaks wonderfully, with varied replies in conversation. Astonishing miracles follow upon remarkable and glorious signs.

17. At the time when a deadly famine ravaged, as it did, all the provinces, a certain boy, almost dead of hunger, threw himself at the knees of the saint with faint breath, and begged him to have pity on him. The man full of piety, taking pity on him, looked at the one who was in charge of the house and said: ‘I commend this boy to you with the greatest care, under the witness of Christ.’ Then he promised that he would apply diligence as he was instructed; but while he was kept busy here and there with various occupations, he began to treat the destitute boy somewhat less carefully. The boy, worn out by cold and hunger, threw himself into the furnace of the baths, and since with his faint breath he could no longer drag his already exhausted limbs, at last he lost his breath and died. The servant, having questioned everyone, at length searched everywhere, and nowhere found any trace of the boy. But the blessed bishop asked the servant for the one entrusted to him. He, prostrate at his knees, confessed that he had lost him. At once the blessed man went into his cell, cast himself on the ground, poured out abundant tears, redoubled deep sighs, and besought the Lord Jesus that [the boy] be restored to his sight. For he had taken what he heard so hard, and let out such weeping with cries, as if mourning his own crime, as though the soul of the dead were already being required from his hands before the tribunal of the eternal Judge. Meanwhile the one whose duty it was hurried to light the furnace, and finding the corpse, tried to drag out the stiff limbs, and recognising [the boy] lifeless, he reported it to the blessed bishop. Again he lay prostrate on the ground and groaned, poured out prayers, remained long in sighs, and raising his head over the bones of the lifeless one, ordered warm water to be poured over [them]. Meanwhile the priest of God, beating his breast, besought the Lord for him without ceasing. The limbs of the dead boy began to move little by little, and the bones, serving their uses, returned to their former function. And though [still] weak, while the blessed man continued in prayer, he afterwards rolled himself to his feet, and on touching his footprint he regained his former strength. So he is believed to survive the ruin of the famine to this day: for he stayed with us for a long time afterwards.

18. Before many years had passed, another deed divinely done by him is also recorded. There was a certain pool on the small estate of the Virisionenses, abundant in its mass of water, as being consecrated to demons: and if anyone for any reason entered it, he was suddenly entwined in demonic cords and cruelly lost his life. But God’s help came at last with the arrival of blessed Sulpicius. Then the inhabitants of the place, clinging to the saint’s knees, begged that the priest would come to the aid of his people, for they lamented that they had lost many kinsmen and servants there. He, as always, pitying them with all his heart, ordered chrism to be mixed with oil and a little water; and blessing it, he gave it to a disciple, instructing him to say, after the example of the prophet Elisha: ‘Thus says the Lord: I have healed these waters, and there shall no longer be in them death or barrenness’ (4 Kings 2:21). When this had been done, the most wicked enemy was suddenly so put to flight that from then on everyone crosses in good fortune, and they draw an abundance of fish onto the shore, and no one experiences danger. So health was restored to the people, and the sickness of the water was taken away.

19. Not long after there follows a far more illustrious act of power. When one of the country folk had of his own accord thrown himself into the river to relieve the summer heat, he was at once bound in Satan’s snares and his life was violently cut off. This place lies not far from the house of the basilica, where the saint of God was reclining with the brothers for a meal in a certain exedra. Meanwhile an old woman was standing at a distance, and suddenly beckoned with her hand to the servants who stood in the bishop’s sight. They tried to find out through one of their fellow servants what the sign meant, and when he came to the place, the woman showed that someone, sunk into the depths, had lost his breath. Then he called his companions and reported to the bishop, who ordered the body to be drawn out and kept until the Ninth Hour. And when all had eaten, he went to the place of prayer. And indeed, had he asked at once, he would have drawn out life from the lifeless; but he thought three hours should pass from the Sixth, so that no one might doubt that the man had truly been dead. At length he rose from prayer and ordered the lifeless man to be set before him, and raising his hand he impressed the image of the cross; and with breath recovered, the dead man’s limbs moved here and there: and so at the bishop’s word he quickly rose up unharmed, and with his strength restored he went back on his own feet.

20. At one time one of the nobles, named Theodegisil, came to visit the blessed bishop. He showed him the affection he was known to bestow on all; and since it was winter, too much fuel was heaped on the fire. The servants’ minds were perhaps occupied with something else; no one was concerned about the danger of fire. At length the flame swiftly devoured the roof, and now, everything being sprinkled [with fire], all began to shake, and with collapse threatening they found the flames strong: the abundant fire had thrown everyone into terror. Since because of the great difficulty no one dared to climb onto the roof, all, despairing of help, took to flight. The priest, with the standard of the cross in his hand, strove to resist the flames, and to the amazement of all the balls of flame were at once so extinguished, before the servant of God drew back his hand, as if they had been surrounded on every side by the rush of the waters of a great river.

21. Let us relate a deed like this one. Within the walls of the city a certain woman of rank had filled a great barn with ears of grain. In the dead of night a criminal stealthily entered, and when he set fire to it the flames soon surrounded [it]. Nor could it stay hidden, for the grief of all made it known: an uproar broke out where the blessed man lay sunk in his usual sleep. At length, having learned from a disciple the cause of what had happened, he went at swift pace and circled the blaze of flames with spiritual songs. In a wonderful manner he fixed with his staff a boundary, a fiery mound which it could not cross. While [the flames] were touching the adjoining houses on every side, they turned back on themselves and were drawn together into one; they fled to a gulf beyond which they did not dare to pass. The Father, exulting, returned rejoicing to the church, to pay the due praises at the morning hours.

22. Let us add a third deed like these miracles. The man of God had built with the greatest effort a certain monastery in the same city, in which he had enclosed a company of virgins and continent women; there he raised a structure of stone with ancient buildings. Through the carelessness of someone, when the silence of night had fallen, [a fire], having caught on a wall, spread, growing little by little; soon, the house having collapsed, it was getting ready to reach the neighbouring ones. And now the mass of flames had grown into a great mountain. At length the priest of God, summoned by his sheep, hastened to the folds; he prepared to resist the flames, of immense height, with the sign of the cross. At once in the middle of the blaze holy help appeared in the form of a dove, in which the Holy Spirit had descended upon the Lord when he was baptized. Suddenly the flames were checked and did not dare to touch the other houses. The shepherd instructed the rescued sheep with saving counsels, and through his teaching the resolve of chastity shines among them to this day. While they eagerly devote themselves to the pursuit of wisdom, they consecrate not only their bodies but also their souls by the grace of virginity, preparing clean vessels for wisdom, from which they seek the holy and immortal unions of the divine Word, from which an offspring may be left in no way subject to the corruption of mortality; and how greatly the grace of abstinence, sobriety and modesty shines among them with fair beauty, it is beyond our powers to declare. Now let us return to the thread of our narrative.

23. Far from the city, at a place called Anatra, he ordered a huge tree to be cut down with axes; when by this action it was cut through and fell swiftly, one of the boys, his mind occupied with something else and standing dazed, foolishly did not flee death. At once the priest raised his hand with the sign of the cross, and wonderfully turned the tree to the other side, and drew the boy safe out of the danger of death.

24. And now, while miracles shone like the brightest stars, and faith flourished, by which everywhere all alike had believed in the Lord the Saviour, that rival of all goodness and ancient deceiver of the human race strove, through certain wicked men, to attack with internal war the Church resting in peace, together with all the people; and he inflamed a certain prince of the provinces of the Gauls with the fire of greed, and urged him with secret persuasions to enrol the people of Bourges, together with the priests of the Church, in an abominable census: and like some beast hissing with a double mouth and darting diabolical poisons with two tongues, he sent one of his agents to harass the said people. But since divine power and grace never desert their own, above all in the greatest struggle, when the abominable minister, under royal cruelty, tried to force into servitude the Christian multitude which had remained free for ages, all, unable to bear the impious affliction, such a multitude flocked to the holy shepherd, and so great a din of lamenters with raised voices broke out, that it was thought a terrible thunder to those who heard it. The voices of all cried out this alone: ‘Holy shepherd, help the flock which until now you have cherished with pastoral affection. Act, lest the flock entrusted to you by God perish: defend it from the wolf who tears it with rabid tooth.’ Then he, moved by great compassion, proclaimed a fast for all, and spoke gently to the assessor, that he might stop carrying out the impious order. But when the mind hardened by pride was not broken, and, scorning the priest’s words, grew hotter and hotter, the blessed man went to his cell, prostrated himself on the ground, beat his holy breast with blows, and asked of the Lord what he had been unable to obtain from the governor. And knowing that it is no lesser virtue of soul to pray to the Lord for an enemy than to fall down for the Lord, he asked for the conversion of his enemies rather than their ruin. And indeed, had he asked, a fitting and outstanding punishment of the immoderate prince and the most savage assessor would at once have come; but the blessed man was always gentle and kind towards his adversaries.

25. Meanwhile he sent one of his own, a certain solitary named Ebregisil (who, renouncing all things, that is, the world with all that was his, was more outstanding than the rest in life and speech after the example of the blessed man), to rebuke the cruelty of the prince, and to announce to him that, unless he changed by the amendment of a better life, sudden death was hanging over him. The blessed man's follower also added, warning the prince about the impieties of the crimes he had committed, whether perhaps he might do penance for what he had committed, whether he might weep for his crime and quench the avenging punishments of the flames with an abundance of tears; for God does not so much will the death of sinners as that they be converted and live. When the king heard this, he was terrified with great fear, and shaken with such dread that at once, acknowledging his guilt, mourning his offence with tears, doing penance without royal pride, he willingly fulfilled what had been made known by so great a priest through his disciple. Swiftly the unaccustomed tax was abolished, the impious assessment was rescinded, safety was granted to the people; and as if the splendour of the sun had been restored after a great storm, peace was given to the Church and the joys of the priests were heaped up. Wonderfully, too, the king added that a general decree should be issued, so that the impious levy should not be repeated upon the people in future. But a fitting vengeance struck the savage assessor, who had not given assent to the king's instruction, and he at once lost with disgrace the life he unworthily enjoyed. For the minister of so great a sacrilege could not escape unpunished. O man blessed in all things! who never defended himself against the fury of his adversaries by hand or weapon, but by fasts and continual vigils, placed beneath the altar, through supplication he secured God as defender for himself and for his Church. And who could ever frighten him with his schemes or assaults, who always remained safe and unconquered by the helping right hand of Christ?

26. At that same time the man of God, observing apostolic simplicity in all things, inferior to none, and in all things perfect, truly a priest and a victim of God, was striving to complete the work he had long since undertaken, everywhere solicitous for the feeding of the poor; and as his age, now full, was sinking towards decrepit old age, he saw that he was not sufficient for everything: either to be free for the deeper things of God, or to remain continually in holy prayers as he wished, or to carry out the instruction of those who were daily being restored to the faith; from all of which not even a breath, nor at least one free hour of time, was given him, since he was always being called from some things to others, so that from first light until deep evening he never ceased to be held in various occupations. When therefore he saw himself weighed down by so great a burden, he judged it more useful to hand over a share of his office and labour to one of the faithful Christian leading men of the region, a man already fully and excellently instructed, Wlfelentus [another reading: Vulfolendus], and to entrust to him at least the ministry of the divine word; and so, with the clergy assembled, [this man] received there the rights of the priesthood.

27. Who could relate with what humility, with what charity he was content thereafter to show himself towards his companions and ministers and in the support of the poor? He was always ruminating with most pure mouth on that saying of the Gospel, and striving with all his strength to fulfil it in deed: ‘Whoever wishes to be your first, let him be your last; and whoever wishes to be your lord, let him be your servant’ (Matth. 20:26). And because he had the eye of his mind wholly fixed on God, he unfailingly considered that our Lord Jesus Christ, made man for our sake, had taught us this: that we should struggle against sin even unto death. For he himself did not think it robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself even unto death. Following him, Sulpicius, God's saint, took upon himself the labours of all hardships and the torments of flesh and mind, so that his conscience might not stain its resolve of faith.

28. Since indeed, if we wish now to relate the miracles of the most blessed bishop Sulpicius and to set out the strength of his constancy, we have neither the abundance of speech for so great a task, nor do we think they would seem credible to others, except to those alone who saw them with their own eyes, let our discourse now run on to those things it had begun earlier, so that we may endeavour to weave together a few of the miraculous deeds which, after he had joined a partner to himself, he thereafter performed by the power of heaven. On one occasion one of the wicked, being, as it were, needy, violently broke by night into the storeroom of the blessed man; at once he tried to carry off what in his savage mind he had conceived as the crime of theft; and while he hurried to leave, no exit for returning lay open, and, enclosed as if in a prison built with every fortification, the guilty man was bound on every side. So having spent the whole night's journeying in vain, he to whom the entry had been easy found not even the slightest way back. Meanwhile the splendour of daylight lit up the world, and the man of God called one of the keepers and, sending him to his companion, ordered him to drag out the man he would find in the storeroom, worn out by wandering and, as if held tight by certain bonds, thus entangled in his crime.

29. Without delay the servant hurried to his companion; having called him, they found the criminal inside and at once seized him to drag him out. Slippery, he suddenly slipped out of their hands; and when he saw himself hemmed in by his crimes and surrounded on all sides by crowds, preferring to undergo a swift death rather than drag out the torments of a long punishment for his crime, he threw himself headlong, to perish, into a well of nearly eighty cubits which was nearby. Nevertheless, when the devouring earth [perhaps: water] had received him, he begged for the intercession of the blessed bishop. Then the man of God, arriving with swift haste, ordered one of the boys, tied [with a rope], to go down after the fallen man, warning him to take the greatest care to draw up the criminal holding him in his arms. And when all cried out that the one whom so deep a chasm of the earth had swallowed could no longer be alive, but rather he was believed by all to have already perished, he commanded the boy to obey his orders swiftly. The servant went in without hesitating, armed with the sign of the holy man, and found lively the one whom all believed to be lifeless. Bound with ropes, he brought the captive back to his native ground. The walls were packed with crowds of people; almost the whole city had flowed together to the spectacle of so great a thing; with clapping of hands the voices of all resounded; they marvelled to see safe the one whom they had thought already dead, sunk in a pit of such depth. Then the criminal, shaken by deep amazement of mind, prostrated at the holy feet, begged pardon for his crime. At once the man full of compassion forgave him, and gave him what was necessary for his needs, often warning him rather to ask than to seize, and to wish things to be given him as a gift, not by robbery. See how perfect was the humility in him, how ready the mercy, how holy the simplicity: and who could say how great was his patience and long-suffering?

30. When one of his disciples of the order of deacons asked leave to return home, he, out of affectionate love, lest something should happen by chance on the long journey, did not grant him freedom to depart. But this man, armed with the spirit of pride, when the first sleep had scarcely loosened forgetfulness of cares, with hurried step, his offence driving him on, took to flight with a vehicle; and he was struck with the fitting punishment of blindness, so that he ran this way and that through the whole night uncertain, with empty labour. When day was restored to the earth, his course spent in vain, he saw that he was standing at the place where he had hastily set out. At length he came to the priest, from whom, I think, nothing was now hidden, begged pardon for his offence, clung to the holy knees, and confessed what had happened in order. That mind most ready in compassion forgave him, and at once granted pardon to the one confessing.

31. Indeed, for those who desire to know with how great an effort and with what arts the most wicked demon with his whole army fought against him, and how, beyond all the others who at that time were struggling for the name of Christ, he brought forth new devices and stirred up the weapons of demonic fury against him, we have taken care to touch briefly on a few things. And since we have already spoken a little earlier of his frequent night vigils: when in the deep silence of a certain night he had completed the singing of psalms in the baptistery, he went with a few [companions] to the basilica of Blessed Martin, to feast there in divine praises for the rest of the night until Matins. And when, with a boy going before with a lamp, he had already reached the doors of the basilica, the deadly demon thrust himself forward in powerful form and in the likeness of a most foul and horrible bird, first tried to put out the light going ahead, then flung himself with great force into the face and eyes of the blessed man, and, flying around this way and that at a distance with ridiculous attempts, again and again made himself violent and hostile. At this the man of God, thinking little of these deeds, said: ‘I know who you are, minister of the ancient serpent, and you do not let yourself be hidden, you who show yourself almost continually as a most wicked persecutor.’ At length, when he raised his hand with the sign of the cross, not only did [the demon] not dare to mingle further, but at the stroke [another reading: thrust] of the cross imprinted [on him] he vanished thus.

32. Since the deception had been shameless and pitiful, the rebellious enemy then, goaded on, kindled very great fury to do injury to the holy man. So when he had ordered one of the boys, simple in mind and manner of life, named Ansulf, to go to a certain place to obtain the food needed for the brothers and the poor, without delay he obeyed the orders, carried out the commands, and hurried to return home. The most savage demon with his attendants put himself in his way: he threw him from the vehicle, and left him lifeless, badly beaten with whips; half-alive, that is, he was carried home by those close to him. And since, because of the injury [done] to Saint Sulpicius, no one reported what had happened, he at length perceived, through the spirit of prophecy which he had received by the grace of the Godhead, that his servant had remained for ten days on end mute and blind, with all his limbs as if dead, and his mouth so locked with his teeth that no one could pour a drop of water inside. Meanwhile the man of God told the brothers in order what he had perceived in spirit, and grieving for the afflicted man out of affection, and shedding tears out of compassion, the loving shepherd lamented that the sheep had suffered torments on his account. At once, however, he prostrated his holy limbs on the ground, and, rising from the earth after prayer, ordered a morsel of bread with wine to be offered to the lifeless man: immediately, his teeth having been opened with iron, those close to him poured into his mouth a drop of the wine which [another reading: that] he had sent. Soon the lost senses were restored to the man who had been in great part as if dead, and his limbs returned to their former vigour and service. This indeed we learned from the very one who suffered it, confirmed by the testimony of the faithful.

33. Not long after, when the setting of the day had come to the earth, Blessed Sulpicius went into the church with a few [companions] to spend the night, and when deep quiet had come, the cunning of the serpent first soothed [them] in the air with a faint hissing. Then, since it was everywhere, with a powerful onslaught it shook the enclosure of the church, the arches, the altars, the lamps and the other furnishings, so that the disciples thought the church was being overturned from its foundations; and trembling and pale with excessive fear, abandoning the chants, expecting destruction, they clung to the pavement. But the Blessed one, unconquered in all things, persisted so bravely in the divine chants, thinking little of what the envious one was doing, that he had never been steadier or more radiant in prosperity. At length the envious serpent gathered himself with his army into one mass, and thinking to frighten off that unbroken constancy with heavier blows and noise, resounding with immense tumult he flung himself on the pavement before the face of the blessed man, so that the disciples thought their master had been crushed to pieces. They indeed remained stunned for a long time; but the glorious priest, wounding the adversary with divine darts, persevered in spiritual chants. He did, however, rebuke the disciples for having abandoned the chants, frightened off by phantom threats. But what wonder if this enemy of the human race sought the death of so great a priest, since he was leader and standard-bearer among the people of God, when he once even stretched out his wicked and impure outrages to the injury of the Godhead itself?

34. And since malice fights unceasingly against goodness, and the jealousy of the adversary pursues the saints of God, we are not able to tell how much the most wicked enemy, showing himself in various illusions, is said to have heaped up the goads of his fury against the flock of Christ, which His right hand protected through His priest. Yet let us relate in a brief account one of the things which, as is believed, he did against one of the servants of Christ, with so many witnesses. When one of the band of those whose duty it is to sing continually to God in the Mother church, named Legontius, was going in his due course to keep the night vigil at the church, he met the enemy of the human race as a warrior against him; and the adversary, gnashing his teeth in anger, tried to call the servant of God back from the journey of good work he had begun, and, having afflicted him with many blows, left him half-alive and almost lifeless; and when he was found in the morning lying on the ground by many, all his senses had lost the service of their function. At that time the saint of God had gone away far from the city, and when he returned after three days, he found him half-alive and badly beaten with whips. Then, prostrating himself beside the brother's body, he groaned loudly, and, the teeth having been opened by force, the priest of God poured the sacrifice into his mouth with his own hands. And while all looked on in wondering amazement, at once, his hand being grasped, he rose up unharmed before the face of the priest, as if he were thought to have suffered no harm; and leaping about everywhere he blessed the Lord.

35. Not long after, one of the country people, taking an axe in his hand, defiled the day of the Lord's resurrection with wicked work: at once the sacrilegious hand withered, the skin dried up with the sinews, and the axe was shut in, stuck fast. Immediately he hurried to the saint of God and rolled himself at the feet of Christ's athlete: the withered hand betrayed the author of the sacrilege, and [the saint] advised the guilty man rather to go to the church weeping. The priest continued prayers beneath the altar, so that at length he might obtain from Christ pardon for the crime he had committed. Meanwhile the saint of God had recourse to his customary defence: he entered his cell sprinkled with ashes, and spent the night in prayer, shedding tears; and when in the morning the priest of God had come to the church to render the due praises, while a varied crowd looked at the man with the axe, the man of God bent down, prostrate in prayer: and suddenly the guilty man, unable to bear the torment, resounded with such great cries that the place was thought to be shaken. For an immense fear seized everyone. Meanwhile the sacrilegious hand was suddenly restored to its former function, the bones, skin and sinews were filled again with their moisture, and the axe sprang away from that hand to one side, wonderfully: the criminal poured out abundant tears, confessed his sin and was absolved, and returned home absolved. Thus divine providence, excelling in mercy, sets right the diseases of the soul by the affliction of the body, according to that [saying]: I will visit their iniquities with the rod; but my mercy I will not take away from them (Psalm 88:33).

36. And since our Lord and Saviour, when long ago placed on earth, had said to the disciples: If you believe in me, the works which I do you also shall do, and greater than these you shall do (John 14:12), the spiritual flame had at last kindled the blessed man so greatly to the love of faith that if anyone secretly snatched the water dripping from his hands while he was washing, and touched the body of any sick person, [that person] was freed from many infirmities; but especially those troubled with tertian and quartan fevers recovered their former health, to [everyone's] wondering amazement. For how great or what signs the Lord worked through him at the last, and made manifest by new and astonishing miracles of power, we think would be credible to none but those alone who saw them with their own eyes.

37. And since he was believed to have fellowship of life and deeds not with other mortals but with the immortal angels, he so greatly rejected the deceit and allurements of the world that he could rightly say with the Apostle: For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain (Philippians 1:21); and that [other saying]: I desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ (ibid. 23), except that he wished to live for the sake of those for whom [he wished] also to die. In short, he rejected the pomp of the world like dung, despised gold, and spurned silver like mud. He held councils, summoned bishops to synods, and warned them often not to neglect the divine commandments, repeating in full that commandment of the Saviour: Do not possess gold nor silver, etc. (Matthew 10:9). But according to the Apostle, having, he says, food and clothing, let us be content with these (1 Timothy 6:8), and the things that follow are to be shunned. He himself laboured with all his strength, chastising his body and bringing it into subjection, lest perhaps while he preached to others he himself should become reprobate. For a long time Blessed Sulpicius had no silver vessels, nor used them, but everything for his use was of wood, earthenware and marble. O unbroken constancy! which by the virtue of patience trampled on the base things by which human frailty is assailed. And since, according to the word of the Saviour (Matthew 5:9), he taught those things which he himself had first done in all respects, no one doubts that he was great in the kingdom of heaven. He was a priest of God wearing the pontifical plate, who by crucifying his body in himself and pursuing vices obtained a new martyrdom, not by death but by the mortification of the flesh.

38. And when he had now built churches, monasteries and cells amply and abundantly, having become father of innumerable clerics and monks, very many renouncing their possessions, who, devoted to this kind of philosophy, having distributed their goods to all the needy, and casting far away even the many cares of life, were living outside the city in little gardens or in any small plots of land; while others, like those who first believed in the Acts of the Apostles, are recorded to have led their life, selling their possessions and estates, and laying the prices at the feet of the others, it being divided to each as there was need; so that he might readily fulfil the gospel duty, [he had] all whom he had desired most fully instructed in spiritual teachings, and so devoted to the studies of Christian philosophy in imitation of their master that some even after three days allowed the body food, not so much desired as necessary; that is, while many, occupied in the deeper understanding of the sacred books, as though gaping at plentiful feasts, could not be satisfied, and were more keenly inflamed by contemplating, and with continual struggle so contended against the flesh as to yield in nothing to its pleasure and lust, while ever more earnestly feeding the soul on the pastures of wisdom and the food of knowledge. The Father, exulting at such zeal of his sons, at length hastened to claim from the eternal Father the interest laid up [for him]. And suddenly the Lord was present to console and reward his faithful servant.

39. And while he shone with these miracles of power, the glorious time of his blessed consummation arrived. But though his limbs, now broken by age, were failing, the burden of abstinence strengthened his afflicted and deadened body; and what nature had neglected, merit made firm. And so, full of days, the time of his life completed, flashing with the splendour of his merits, he committed his earthly limbs to the earth, [and] his heavenly spirit ascended to the heights of heaven among the choirs of angels.

40. Then from every side of the city a crowd of countless peoples suddenly flowed together from everywhere: the walls, the courts and all the streets were packed, so much so that, had the help of the blessed bishop not been present, the greater part of the people, trampled underfoot, their breath violently cut off, would have been killed by the crush of so many. The lamentation of all was immense, the grief unbearable, and those mourning broke out in their voices with such groaning that even hearts of stone poured forth immense weeping. I do not know whether anyone there was so cruel and senseless that he could have held himself back from tears. For so great a crash of voices resounded that that place was thought to be shaken as if by a great thunderclap. And since the grief of soul of all was without limit, the sobs of the clergy were utterly broken, [and] despondent lamentation scarcely allowed them to sing the spiritual hymns; the groaning of those grieving forced out only these words between sobs: Alas, desolate flock, what will you do? See, your shepherd lost, you are scattered, and who will ever be able to free you from the raging teeth of the wolves? In your death, then, O good shepherd, who could doubt that we have all perished?

41. Meanwhile they came to the basilica where now the priest of God, awaiting the time of the resurrection in glorious triumph, lies buried in wondrous beauty, [the basilica] which he himself had long ago built with the greatest effort. When the body had been brought to the tomb, the whole people, unable to bear the absence of their shepherd, lying prostrate on the pavement, gave forth a bellowing beyond human measure, so much so that even the ministers of the church were not allowed freedom to perform the office. They mourned as absent him whom they had not lost but sent ahead, plainly not knowing that, entering heaven, he was hastening to discharge an embassy on their behalf before the divine gaze, so that there he might intercede for the people, which here he would repay to the one who asked in faith; there he might pour out prayers, which here he would answer to [their] prayers.

42. Nor did he suffer for long to be absent from those whom, while placed on earth, he had cherished with unceasing labour, but at once he hastened in spirit to visit those whom he had left in body, not in affection. And so suddenly, by restoring health in various infirmities, he showed himself to be present, as if a light shown from heaven, or some ray of the sun bursting forth, lit up the whole world with the brightness of the light on high; whereupon through all the cities and villages immense multitudes of people gathered to the churches, as wheat is gathered to the threshing-floors at harvest time. And not only to the neighbouring cities, but even to all the kingdoms of the earth, his most brilliant fame for the various miracles of healing shone forth as if in winged flight. And had the basilica itself not been greatly enlarged, it could not have held the multitude of the sick within its space. And if I am found worthy to have God as my guide, I wish yet to set out in a short discourse some of the things which the outstanding victor has now done. And quite fittingly the place where these things are done is called by the ancient predecessors NAVIS, "Ship", on account of the harbour for shipping; this name formerly indicated, as if by a kind of presage of things to come, what it now shows by divine favour. For this is the Ship in which those who cling to it cross the sea of this world and arrive free at the far-off homeland, namely of the heavenly kingdom. There indeed a harbour of refuge is made from the threatening storms of evils, visible and invisible; there the grace of escaping from the waves of the world and the tempests of whirlwinds is granted. There daily they pour the salt of knowledge into the weak and the ignorant; there, through the intercession of our blessed Father, healing of the sick is granted freely by the eternal and invisible physician; through it the shipwrecked and exiles return to their former homeland.

43. Leaving aside, then, the other things, to which I shall attend shortly, as I promised above, I shall now speak briefly of the lamp that hangs before the tomb of the Blessed [man]. It is said to have been filled with oil once by the ministers, and, the holy liquid overflowing, to pour out an abundance from above in a continual stream, with which many who were anointed are said to have been freed from many various infirmities. And this must be told not without wonder, that once in the evening, while the company of priests was resounding with divine songs, suddenly a heavenly flame, with a stroke like lightning, struck the fuel of the lamp and wondrously gave light as all looked on, and never afterwards lost its brightness, which [flame], kindled by divine ministry, its fuel nourishes to this day.

44. To these deeds of a most illustrious man, although they have been set out in unworthy words, we now resolve at a fitting time to put an end; we lay our hand upon our mouth, we hasten to return inward to our conscience. And him whom we cannot imitate let us ask to become our patron, that we may be helped by the merits of him whose heavenly birthday we celebrate, with the help of him who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, God, through all ages of ages. Amen.
